title: Autocallable Options Pricing with Integration-Based Exponential Amplitude Loading
abstract_summary: The paper presents a complete quantum algorithm for pricing autocallable (path-dependent) options, introducing an improved integration-based exponential amplitude loading technique that reduces circuit depth and T-depth for the payoff component. The authors provide complexity analysis showing up to ≈50x T-depth reduction in a relevant setting, and validate the approach with end-to-end circuit implementations and simulations on HPC resources (up to 33 qubits), demonstrating empirical convergence toward classically estimated values.
methodology_description: The paper develops and implements an end-to-end quantum algorithm for pricing single-asset autocallable options (with generalization to multi-asset). The approach combines: (1) Gaussian re-parameterization state preparation (variational Gaussian loaders) per time step to encode log-return samples; (2) quantum arithmetic (in-place adders) to accumulate log-returns across time steps and evaluate barrier crossing and binary-option conditions in log-return space using comparators; (3) an improved integration-based exponential amplitude loading method (partial exponential state preparation on a restricted interval plus a comparator/integrator) to map from log-return space to payoff amplitudes without degrading the post-processing normalization; (4) controlled Ry rotations to encode constant payoffs and to remap normalization factors; and (5) Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) to estimate the expected discounted payoff (probability of the QAE target qubit being |1>). They provide an analytical T-depth and error-budgeting analysis (truncation, discretization, approximation, arithmetic, amplitude-loading errors) and compare T-depths against a QSP-based baseline. Circuits were synthesized via the Classiq platform / Qmod and executed on statevector / shot-based simulators (Classiq default simulator, Nvidia single-GPU simulator, and Cirq+cuQuantum on the LEONARDO HPC) for a small proof-instance. They benchmark results against classical baselines: (i) traditional Monte Carlo, (ii) Monte Carlo with the same Gaussian discretization, (iii) closed-form with Gaussian discretization, and (iv) closed-form with discretization and fixed-point arithmetic precision matching the quantum model.

experiment_input.preprocessing: Gaussian truncation (smin=3) and discretization performed to build k-qubit approximation of standard normal per timestep; affine transform applied to obtain desired mean/variance; accumulation of log-returns via in-place addition; partial exponential state prepared on specified interval for integration amplitude loading.

pipeline_steps: 1) For each time step prepare a discretized standard Gaussian state using variational Gaussian loaders (one register per timestep).
2) Affine-transform Gaussian samples (mean and variance) to produce per-step log-return increments and accumulate them in-place across timesteps using quantum adders to form cumulative log-returns.
3) Update barrier-crossing register (Ct) and binary-option indicator register (Bt) using comparators on the accumulated log-returns (log-space comparisons).
4) For binary payouts: apply controlled Ry rotations on the QAE target qubit conditioned on binary indicators to load constant (discounted) binary payoffs directly into amplitude.

5) For the knock-in put payoff (non-constant): prepare a partial exponential reference state on the relevant interval (restricted to [x0,x1]) and perform the integration comparator to load a mapping of exp(log-return) into the amplitude (improved integration amplitude loading).
6) Apply an Ry rotation to remap normalization so that amplitude range [0,1] corresponds to chosen payoff mapping (includes mapping zero payoff to a nonzero loaded amplitude as needed).
7) Use Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) to estimate the probability of the target qubit being |1> (the rescaled expected discounted payoff).
8) Post-process IQAE output with the inverse normalization mapping to obtain the expected payoff in monetary units.

9) Validate results by comparing to classical baselines: traditional Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo with same Gaussian discretization, closed-form with discretization, and closed-form with discretization+fixed-point arithmetic precision matching the quantum circuit.

results_summary: The paper proposes an enhancement to integration-based exponential amplitude loading for quantum pricing of autocallable options, aiming to avoid normalization overestimation by preparing partial exponential reference states. The authors provide a complexity analysis that attributes a large reduction in T-depth of the payoff-loading subroutine relative to prior approaches (they report a ∼50x reduction in a cited 'relevant setting'), present an end-to-end implementation (Classiq/Qmod), and validate behavior via gate-level simulations up to 33 qubits on classical HPC/GPU simulators. Simulator experiments, together with constrained classical benchmarks of discretization and fixed-point arithmetic, show convergence of the quantum-circuit outputs toward classical estimates as precision and discretization are increased. The work is framed as a step toward resource-efficient quantum pricing of path-dependent derivatives, while acknowledging that circuit sizes remain large and that running on real, noisy quantum hardware remains impractical today.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper relies on the standard theoretical quadratic sampling speedup of Quantum Amplitude Estimation over Monte Carlo and presents resource (T-depth) reductions for a key submodule (payoff amplitude loading). However, it does not demonstrate an end-to-end, hardware-executed quantum advantage; the evidence is based on theoretical complexity analysis and classical simulator experiments constrained to small instances.
limitations: Circuit size remains considerable even for small-scale examples, requiring use of simulators rather than real hardware (author-stated).
All experimental validation was performed on simulators (Classiq, Nvidia GPU simulator, LEONARDO HPC) — no empirical runs on quantum hardware due to coherence/fidelity limits (author-stated).
Simulator capacity forced reduction of circuit width/depth for executable instances, limiting experiments to small problem instances (single asset, T=3) and up to 33 qubits (author-stated).
Classical benchmarking was constrained by simulator limits; full classical/quantum comparisons at production-scale discretizations were impractical (author-stated).

The demonstrated improvement primarily reduces T-depth of the payoff (amplitude-loading) component; it may not substantially reduce total T-depth unless other modules are optimized as well (author-stated).

The method and complexity analysis assume parallelization of submodules (e.g., exponential state preparation in parallel with other blocks), which may be challenging to realize on actual hardware (inferred).

The implementation and experiments assume Black–Scholes log-return modeling and Gaussian discretization; applicability/accuracy under more realistic or calibrated models (stochastic/local volatility) is not validated (author-stated and inferred).

Resource and T-depth estimates rely on error-budget allocations and approximations (e.g., truncation/discretization/approximation); practical fault-tolerant resource requirements and overheads (magic-state distillation, routing, etc.) are not fully quantified (inferred).
Scalability to realistic multi-asset, many-timestep autocallables (larger d and T) is not demonstrated experimentally; generalization is discussed but not empirically validated (inferred).
The approach depends on pre-trained variational Gaussian loaders (re-parameterization) — training overhead, robustness and impact on end-to-end accuracy are not analyzed in detail (inferred).

Partial exponential state preparation for non-power-of-two intervals requires exact amplitude amplification (Grover-based), which can introduce nontrivial overheads in practice; the trade-offs are not fully explored experimentally (inferred).
Error-mitigation strategies or concrete methods to make the circuits robust on near-term noisy devices are not provided beyond a call for future testing with mitigation (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Integration-based exponential amplitude loading reduces T-depth (authors report up to ≤50x T-depth reduction versus a QSP-based baseline) in their analytical resource comparison for the payoff-loading component.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Practical pipeline combines variational Gaussian state-preparation (pre-trained/loaders) with quantum arithmetic and IQAE, relying on classical pre/post-processing and circuit synthesis via Classiq (Qmod) — a hybrid QPU-CPU workflow.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — End-to-end circuits synthesized and simulated (statevector and shot-based) up to 33 qubits, with empirical convergence to classically estimated payoffs on small proof instances (single-asset, T=3) demonstrating a simulation-level proof-of-concept.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experimental validation is on classical simulators (Classiq simulator, Nvidia GPU simulator, Cirq+cuQuantum on HPC); no experiments on noisy quantum hardware are reported.

#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations are limited to small problem instances (single-asset, 3 timesteps) and circuits up to 33 qubits; this leaves open whether the approach scales to production-size, multi-asset or longer-maturity autocallable contracts.

#limitation:data-encoding — The method requires discretization and Gaussian truncation (smin=3) plus partial-interval exponential amplitude loading; the paper analyses truncation/discretization and amplitude-loading errors but these encoding costs remain significant.

#limitation:noise — Resource and T-depth analysis emphasizes fault-tolerant metrics (T-depth) but the lack of noisy-hardware experiments means the impact of realistic noise and error-correction/mitigation demands is not empirically assessed.
contradictions: The paper asserts substantial T-depth reductions (≤50x) relative to a QSP-based baseline based on analytical comparison, but the empirical validation is limited to small, simulator-only instances (single-asset, T=3, up to 33 qubits). This creates a tension between claimed resource savings and their demonstrated scalability to production-sized problems.

The authors emphasize elements that suggest near-term practicality (variational Gaussian loaders, small-qubit simulations), while the core estimation step relies on Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) and T-depth-focused resource metrics that are more consistent with fault-tolerant regime assumptions—producing an internal tension about near-term feasibility versus long-term, fault-tolerant applicability.
